content.title: BAA implements stricter qualification standards for Boston Marathon
content.text: Runners across the world hoping to take part in next year's Boston Marathon are either celebrating or grappling with disappointment after the Boston Athletic Association made the race steeped in history and prestige even tougher to qualify for. The B.A.A. began notifying applicants on Tuesday of their acceptance into the 130th Boston Marathon that will be run on Monday, April 20, 2026. The qualifying standards were quickened by 4 minutes and 34 seconds for runners' genders and ages. There were a total of 33,249 qualifier applications received during registration week (Sept. 8-12), the B.A.A. said. Email notices to athletes accepted and not accepted will continue through the coming days, according to the B.A.A., which said that a total of 24,362 qualified applicants have been accepted to date or are in the process of being accepted pending final verification of their qualifying performance. “The sport of marathoning is gaining momentum world-wide, and we recognize the dedication it takes to qualify and earn a spot on the starting line for the Boston Marathon,” B.A.A. President and CEO Jack Fleming said in a statement posted online. “The B.A.A. looks forward to showcasing the spirit of our running community to the thousands of qualifiers who’ve now officially circled Marathon Monday, April 20th, on their racing calendars. Unfortunately, we’re unable to accept all applicants into the event, but we do want to applaud all who train and aspire to participate in the Boston Marathon.” 6:112 reporters on preparing for 26.2 miles Our own Matt Prichard and Malcolm Johnson sat down to discuss how they've been getting ready to run in the Boston Marathon and the charities they're doing it for. Three-time Boston Marathon runner Shana Miller tells NBC10 Boston she's heartbroken after finding out she'll miss out on next year's race. Local In-depth news coverage of the Greater Boston and New England area. “Missed the Boston Marathon cutoff by four seconds,” Miller said. "I was about to go out for a speed workout and had just saw the Boston Marathon post online and sat in my car for an hour and cried before I went out to go for my run. Yeah, it’s hard.” Other runners were cheerful to find out they made it, including Cullen McEachern. “I read like the little blurb and got accepted, so I’m pretty stoked. I’m excited to start training for it,” said the former University of Gonzaga runner, who works at Heartbreak Hill Running Company. "Times are getting faster and that is a good thing. As the sport gets more popular, I think times will just continue to go down.” Sydnie Rivas also works at Heartbreak Hill Running Company and says a lot more people are interested in running. "We sell a lot more shoes," said Rivas, who also ran in college and has seen sales soar. "It’s definitely gained a lot of popularity. Since Covid started, I feel like people were bored at home and just started running and ever since then it has gained more popularity.” The community-spirited race represents resilience. “That’s kind of the allure of Boston, as well," McEachern said. "There’s only X amount of people who qualify and only X amount of people who get under the actual cutoff so it’s a pretty cool achievement to get.” Runners like Miller are discouraged -- but motivated. “Pick myself back up," she said of what she'll do next. "I have my race that's coming in the fall and hopefully I can qualify again and make it for 2027.” Miller's heart isn't the only one that was broken this week. We know next year's race will be much more competitive following the new requirements from the B.A.A. The Boston Marathon field size is set at 30,000 official entrants.
